record.original_question: If T is an invertible frequently hypercyclic operator, must the inverse operator T^{-1} also be frequently hypercyclic?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let X be a separable infinite-dimensional Banach space (or, more generally, a separable Fréchet space) and let T: X → X be a continuous linear operator. The operator T is called frequently hypercyclic if there exists a vector x ∈ X (called a frequently hypercyclic vector) such that for every nonempty open subset U ⊆ X, the set of return times

  N(x, U) = { n ∈ ℕ : T^n x ∈ U }

has positive lower density, i.e.

  liminf_{N → ∞} (1/N) · #{ n ∈ {1, …, N} : T^n x ∈ U } > 0.

Assume that T is invertible (with continuous inverse) and frequently hypercyclic. Question: Must the inverse operator T^{-1} also be frequently hypercyclic?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem has been resolved in the negative by Q. Menet (arXiv:1910.04452, published in J. Inst. Math. Jussieu): there exists an invertible frequently hypercyclic operator on ℓ¹(ℕ) whose inverse is not frequently hypercyclic. An analogous counterexample for U-frequently hypercyclic operators on ℓ^p(ℕ) (1 ≤ p < ∞) was given in arXiv:1904.07485.

status_evidence.title: Inverse of frequently hypercyclic operators
status_evidence.snippet: Construction of an invertible frequently hypercyclic operator on ℓ¹(ℕ) whose inverse is not frequently hypercyclic.
status_evidence.claim: The question is answered in the negative.

status_evidence.title: Inverse of U-frequently hypercyclic operators
status_evidence.snippet: An invertible U-frequently hypercyclic operator on ℓ^p(ℕ) whose inverse is not U-frequently hypercyclic.
status_evidence.claim: Negative answer also holds in the U-frequently hypercyclic setting.

status_evidence.title: Inverse of frequently hypercyclic operators - Cambridge Core
status_evidence.snippet: Published version of the result in J. Inst. Math. Jussieu.
status_evidence.claim: Counterexample published in a peer-reviewed journal.
